_meta.title: Κῆπος — the heads of Epicurus's Garden in Athens, 306 BCE – 2nd c. CE
_meta.note: The nine known heads of the Garden from Epicurus to Patro, numbered by succession, plotted at birthplace. Heads 3, 6, and 9 have no recorded birthplace and are not mapped; head 5 (Basilides) is plotted at a conjectural Tyre with a dashed, 'unconfirmed' marker. Imperial-era heads (Popillius Theotimus, head in 121 CE, and Heliodorus) have no recorded birthplaces and are not mapped.
_meta.sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives, Book 10; Cicero, letters and Philippics; Raubitschek, 'Phaidros and His Roman Pupils,' Hesperia 18 (1949); IG II² 1099; Smith, Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography.

heads.name: Epicurus
heads.bio: Founder of the Garden (Kēpos), a philosophical community outside Athens that admitted women and slaves. He taught that pleasure — understood as freedom from bodily pain and mental disturbance — is the highest good, and that the gods do not meddle in human affairs.
heads.note: Born on Samos to Athenian settler parents; an Athenian citizen.

heads.name: Hermarchus
heads.bio: Epicurus' chosen successor, to whom he left the Garden and his library in his will. He defended the school's doctrines and wrote against rival philosophies.

heads.name: Polystratus
heads.bio: Third head of the Garden; fragments of his work on irrational contempt survive on papyrus from Herculaneum. His birthplace is not recorded.

heads.name: Dionysius of Lamptrai
heads.bio: Fourth head of the Garden, from the Attic deme of Lamptrai. Little of his teaching survives.
heads.note: 'Of Lamptrai,' an Attic deme south of Athens.

heads.name: Basilides
heads.bio: Fifth head of the Garden. His birthplace is not recorded; Barnes and Brunschwig have suggested he may be the Basilides of Tyre known from a mathematical text, but this is only a conjecture.
heads.note: Birthplace unconfirmed — 'possibly Tyre' is a modern suggestion, not attested.

heads.name: Apollodorus
heads.bio: Head of the Garden around 100 BCE, nicknamed 'the tyrant of the Garden' for his prolific and dogmatic writing — he is said to have written over four hundred books. His birthplace is not recorded.

heads.name: Zeno of Sidon
heads.bio: A sharp and systematic Epicurean whom Cicero heard lecture at Athens and called 'the coryphaeus of the Epicureans.' He worked on logic and the foundations of mathematics.
heads.note: Some scholars doubt he was formally head of the Garden.

heads.name: Phaedrus
heads.bio: An Epicurean head and friend of Cicero, from an Athenian family of the deme Berenikidai. His treatise On the Gods influenced Cicero's own writing on the subject.
heads.note: From an Athenian family of the deme Berenikidai.

heads.name: Patro
heads.bio: Successor of Phaedrus as head of the Garden; Cicero, who knew him, interceded to protect the school's property in Athens. His birthplace is not recorded.
